title: Light constraints leave a scale to determine
question: What map can respect both light directions?
recap: Ask for a linear map that keeps light at speed c in both directions along the motion, and space and time must mix. One overall factor is left over; going there and back, and the symmetry of space, fix it at gamma.
premises: The two frames’ axes are parallel, and their origins coincide at time zero.
Space and time are the same everywhere, so the map between coordinates is linear.
The two postulates hold, together with going there and back, the symmetry of space, and continuity at zero speed.
limitations: Keeping one light ray at speed c does not fix every coefficient of the map.
The spacetime interval and matrices check the result later; the 1905 argument does not assume them.

overview.text: Ask for a linear map that keeps light at speed \(c\) in both directions along the motion, and space and time must mix. One overall factor is left over; going there and back, and the symmetry of space, fix it at \(\gamma\).

full.text: The moving origin follows \(x = vt\), so write \(x' = a(v)(x - vt)\). Requiring \(x' = ct'\) on \(x = ct\) and \(x' = -ct'\) on \(x = -ct\) fixes the time combination: \(t' = a(v)(t - vx/c^2)\). An overall scale \(a(v)\) remains.

full.spoken: The light constraints give a common coefficient multiplying x minus vt and t minus vx over c squared.

full.text: Going to the moving frame and back, with speed \(v\) and then \(-v\), must return every event unchanged, which gives \(a(v)\,a(-v)\,(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1\). Space has no preferred direction, so \(a(v) = a(-v)\), and since \(a(0) = 1\) the positive root is the one: \(a(v) = \gamma\).

full.spoken: The Lorentz factor is one over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, giving the standard space and time transformation.

full.returnCaption: Return to the map x′ = γ(x − vt), t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), with its factor γ.
Return to finding the map that respects both light directions.

items: The moving origin sits at \(x = vt\), so \(x'\) must be a multiple of \(x - vt\): write \(x' = a(v)(x - vt)\).
Write the time map as a linear combination too, and require light going right, \(x = ct\), to have \(x' = ct'\), and light going left, \(x = -ct\), to have \(x' = -ct'\).
Solve those two conditions: they force \(t' = a(v)(t - vx/c^2)\) and leave the factor \(a(v)\) open.
Transform to the moving frame and back; the result must be the identity, so \(a(v)\,a(-v)\,(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1\).
Use the symmetry of space, \(a(v) = a(-v)\), so \(a(v)^2 = 1/(1 - v^2/c^2)\).
Take the positive root, since \(a(0) = 1\): \(a(v) = \gamma\), which is real only for \(|v| < c\).

margin.text: Einstein’s own §3 derivation follows a light signal out and back between clocks and solves a differential equation for the moving system’s time \(\tau\); the two-direction argument here is a shorter modern route to the same map. His \(\beta\) is the modern \(\gamma\), and his \(\tau\) is a coordinate time, not the proper time of modern texts.
